label: read2-leanbio-binding
in_my_words: Programs that predict how tightly a drug sticks to a protein score worse than people hoped. The authors ask whether the cause is messy lab measurements or tests that are too easy, and lean towards too-easy tests, without calling it settled.
how_in_my_words: They read papers and downloaded public lab data to see how much repeat measurements disagree. From that they worked out a best-possible score, the ceiling, of about 0.85 to 0.95. They compared it with real scores of about 0.75 to 0.80 on fair tests, and ran a made-up computer experiment. They also wrote four facts as computer-checked proofs. They trained no program of their own, and they list many things they did not check.

test_questions.question: What is the ceiling and roughly how big is it for real drug data?
test_questions.my_answer: The best score any program could get when the lab answers themselves wobble; about 0.85 to 0.95.

test_questions.question: What fraction of standard test cases have a near-twin in the training set?
Did the authors train their own prediction program and what did it score?
Which proteins did the lookup trick do best on?
test_questions.my_answer: Unknown; the sources do not say.

test_questions.question: What is the ceiling for the main benchmark itself?
test_questions.my_answer: Not worked out, because they did not download its lab numbers.

words_i_did_not_know: correlation (only half: the 0 to 1 score, but not how it is computed)
sentences_i_could_not_follow: Fourth, any claim of a score above the ceiling must be wrong for that noise level.
They also assume the program never saw the lab's measurement errors. If a program copies the noisy readings, it can score a perfect 1, and the ceiling no longer applies.
In our sample, which protein it was explained only about 8 to 15 percent of the spread.
Third, energy changes around a closed loop of steps must add up to zero.
The first is a fair test with no look-alike cases that scores right at the ceiling.
what_would_help: Put one plain sentence up front saying what the score numbers mean, with a single clear picture. The proof section is hard to follow: the energy-loop fact never says why it matters here. Explain why a lower ceiling than real scores is a verdict on noise. The text mixes 0.82, 0.85 to 0.95 and 0.75 to 0.80 without a simple chart. The glossary has too many jargon terms and some of them, like Cheng-Prusoff, never appear in the text. The made-up experiment is unclear about what it showed. Say plainly how easy tests and noise are told apart.
